strengths: Presents a unified DiT-based framework (AudioX) capable of handling multiple input modalities (text, video, image, music, audio) and multiple generation/completion tasks within a single architecture, addressing a real limitation of prior domain-specific models.

Introduces two new large-scale caption datasets (vggsound-caps with 190K captions, V2M-caps with 6M captions) via an automated captioning pipeline, which could be a useful community resource if released as promised.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many benchmarks (AudioCaps, VGGSound, AVVP, MusicCaps, V2M-bench) and many tasks (T2A, V2A, T2M, V2M, inpainting, completion, image-to-audio zero-shot), with comparisons against numerous strong recent baselines (AudioLDM2, Tango2, MMAudio, Stable Audio Open, FoleyCrafter, VidMuse, etc.).

Reasonable ablations on masking ratio per modality, masking strategy (input vs. feature masking vs. no masking), and intra-/inter-modal contributions, which support the core design choices (input masking over feature masking).
Good qualitative results (spectrogram comparisons) supporting the quantitative claims, and a user study for subjective evaluation across four representative tasks.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: input masking as a training strategy, multi-modal condition concatenation, and DiT-based audio/music generation are individually already explored in prior works (e.g., masked training in AudioMAE, VideoMAE, feature masking works cited); the main novelty is engineering unification plus new datasets rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The technical presentation of the masking strategy is fairly generic (Sec 4.1-4.2); the paper does not give much theoretical or deeper analysis of why input masking outperforms feature masking beyond one intuitive paragraph, and the ablation is on a single small table without statistical significance or multiple seeds.

The performance across tables is mixed: AudioX is not uniformly SOTA — it under-performs Tango2/MMAudio on several IS/FAD metrics in Table 1 (e.g., AudioCaps and VGGSound T2A rows), while the abstract/claims emphasize consistent SOTA performance, which slightly overstates the results.

Captioning pipeline for the new datasets is automated via Qwen2-Audio without human verification or quality-control metrics (e.g., no measurement of caption accuracy, hallucination rate, or inter-rater checks), raising reproducibility/quality concerns about training/eval data reliability given these captions are used both for training and as ground truth in downstream generation evaluation.

Some experimental details are sparse or hard-to-verify: e.g., how zero-padding for missing modalities during training interacts with masking, effect of proprietary music-caption data not released, and unclear description of how classifier-free guidance is applied across mixed modality combinations.

Reproducibility is limited given code/datasets are only promised as future release ("will be available") rather than provided at submission, and specific hyperparameters (e.g., exact masking schedule mechanics, dataset splits sizes for some private data) are only partly documented.

The paper's related-work/framing claims prior expert or generalist models 'lack flexibility' or 'fail to meet diverse demands,' but doesn't provide a systematic comparison of computational cost/parameter efficiency versus these specialized SOTA baselines, making it hard to assess whether the unification comes at added compute or parameter cost relative to gains.

Table 4 (zero-shot image-to-audio) compares against only two baselines and one simple constructed baseline, and the image modality is stated to have no dedicated training data (treated as a single-frame video), so the claimed generalization is a relatively narrow ancillary result rather than a core contribution backed by strong evidence.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically useful problem — unifying audio and music generation across heterogeneous input modalities (text, image, video, music, audio) within a single DiT-based architecture, rather than training separate specialist models.

The authors curate and (promise to) release two new large-scale caption datasets (vggsound-caps with 190K audio captions and V2M-caps with 6M music captions), which could be useful to the community if actually released with sufficient quality control.

The experimental section is broad, covering many tasks (T2A, V2A, T2M, V2M, audio inpainting, music completion, image-to-audio) and many benchmarks (AudioCaps, VGGSound, AVVP, MusicCaps, V2M-bench), with numerous baseline comparisons.
Ablations on masking ratio and masking strategy (input vs. feature vs. no masking) provide some insight into design choices.
Qualitative spectrogram visualizations are provided to complement quantitative metrics.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: input masking across modalities is a fairly direct application of well-established ideas (BERT/MAE-style masking, classifier-free guidance, multi-modal DiT conditioning) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper largely combines existing components (DiT, pretrained CLIP/T5/Stable-Audio-Open VAE encoders, Qwen2-Audio captioning) into a pipeline without a clearly novel algorithmic insight.

The 'SOTA' claim is inconsistently supported by the tables: in many rows of Table 1 (e.g., AudioCaps T2A IS, AVVP V2A FD/PC, several V2M rows) other baselines (MMAudio, AudioGen, VidMuse, etc.) are underlined or better on multiple metrics, so the claim of achieving SOTA 'across most metrics/tasks' is an overstatement relative to the actual numbers presented.

The two new caption datasets are generated fully automatically via Qwen2-Audio/Qwen-VL prompting without any human verification or quality analysis (e.g., hallucination rate, caption-audio alignment accuracy), which is concerning given known issues with audio/video captioning models producing inaccurate or generic descriptions; this could contaminate downstream training/evaluation.

Several evaluation comparisons appear to use self-constructed or weak baselines (e.g., the 'Caption2Audio' baseline for zero-shot image-to-audio in Table 4 is built by the authors themselves by chaining an image captioner with a T2A model), raising concerns about fairness of comparison and cherry-picked settings.

The mask-strategy ablation (Table A3) shows only marginal differences between 'No Mask' and 'Mask Input' (KL 1.90 vs 1.87, IS 5.26 vs 5.44, FD 22.70 vs 21.78), which does not strongly support the paper's central claim that input masking is a key contributor to performance; the effect size seems too small to justify calling it a 'key innovation.'

Music completion (Table 3) and several other task results are reported without any external baseline comparison, only self-comparison across different input-modality combinations, making it hard to judge how competitive the approach actually is for that task.

There is no explicit Limitations section discussing failure modes, computational cost/training footprint, dataset biases, or generalization limits, nor any discussion of ethical/societal risks (e.g., misuse for generating misleading audio, copyright issues with music generation from copyrighted-style prompts), which is a notable omission for a generative audio/music system.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: the paper states 'code and datasets will be available' but provides no concrete release timeline, license, or verification that the promised 6M V2M-caps and proprietary text-music data will actually be shared, and some training data (e.g., 'private' text-music pairs in Table A1) is not public at all.

Figures such as Fig. 5 (mask-ratio ablation) are hard to interpret due to unclear axis/legend labeling and overlapping curves for different modalities and tasks, weakening the evidentiary value of the ablation.

The overall architectural contribution (concatenating modality embeddings and feeding into a pretrained DiT backbone from Stable Audio Open) is engineering-heavy and incremental relative to prior unified any-to-any generation frameworks (e.g., CoDi, NExT-GPT, MMAudio), and the paper does not clearly articulate what specific technical difficulty is uniquely solved beyond scaling up multi-task training with masking.

strengths: Presents a unified DiT-based framework (AudioX) capable of handling multiple input modalities (text, video, image, music, audio) for both audio and music generation, addressing a real limitation of prior domain-specific/single-modality models.

Curates and will release two new large-scale caption datasets (vggsound-caps with 190K audio captions, V2M-caps with 6M music captions), which is a valuable contribution to the community beyond the model itself.

Proposes and validates an input-masking strategy across modalities (rather than feature masking used in prior cross-modal work), with a clear ablation (Table A3) showing input masking outperforms no masking and feature masking.

Extensive experimental evaluation spanning many tasks (T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, TV2M, audio inpainting, music completion, zero-shot image-to-audio) and many datasets/baselines, generally achieving SOTA or comparable results across most metrics.

Includes both objective metrics (KL, IS, FD, FAD, PC, PQ, alignment scores) and a subjective user study, plus ablations on mask ratio and intra-/inter-modal performance, giving a fairly comprehensive evaluation.
Qualitative results (Appendix Figures A1, A2) support the quantitative claims with spectrogram comparisons across tasks.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core architecture is a fairly standard DiT with modality-specific encoders/projections and a masking pretext task; masked training strategies for cross-modal representation learning (masked autoencoders, AudioMAE, VideoMAE, BERT-style masking) are well established, so the main claimed innovation is largely a combination/adaptation of existing ideas to a new domain rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The mask ratios and other hyperparameters (0.6 for video/audio, 0.2 for text) appear tuned somewhat post-hoc based on ablation on the same benchmarks used for final results; it's unclear whether these generalize or were selected via a proper held-out validation protocol, raising some risk of overfitting to the reported test sets.

Some comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples: e.g., in Table 1 AudioX is compared against many specialized single-task/single-modality baselines, but it's not always clear whether these baselines were retrained/fine-tuned on the same curated caption data or evaluated with their original public checkpoints, which could bias comparisons in AudioX's favor given it benefits from newly curated large-scale captions that competitors did not have access to.

The paper lacks discussion of computational cost/efficiency comparisons (inference speed, model size vs. baselines) despite using 250 diffusion steps and a 2.4B parameter model, which is relevant to practical significance.

Limited analysis of failure cases or limitations of the approach (e.g., when input modalities conflict, or when video/audio semantic alignment is weak); the paper only reports successes, which reduces confidence in a full understanding of the method's boundaries.
The user study is quite small in scale (10 users, 25 samples per task) and lacks statistical significance testing or details on rater qualification/inter-rater agreement.

Writing/notation could be tightened in places (e.g., minor Table A1 typos such as 'Vaycaps'), and some architectural details (e.g., exact temporal transformer design for visual projection, how images are distinguished from padded video frames at inference) could be described more precisely for reproducibility.

strengths: Presents a genuinely unified framework (AudioX) that handles arbitrary combinations of text, video, and audio conditioning for both general sound-effect and music generation, addressing a real gap where prior work is largely single-modality or single-domain.

Introduces a large-scale (7M+ sample) structured-annotation dataset (IF-caps) with rich fields (caption, category/count, sound-event-detection timestamps, temporal relations) built via a two-stage Gemini+Qwen2-Audio pipeline, which is a substantial data contribution likely useful to the community if released.
The Multimodal Adaptive Fusion (MAF) module is lightweight (60M params) and is validated with reasonably thorough ablations (gate vs. query components, comparison to w/o MAF).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning many tasks (T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, TV2M, audio inpainting, music completion, zero-shot image-to-audio) and datasets, with both objective metrics and a human subjective study (10 expert raters).

Proposes a new instruction-following benchmark (T2A-bench) with a structured, reasonably well-documented automated evaluation pipeline (blind annotation + LLM judgment), addressing an underexplored aspect (fine-grained controllability) of audio generation evaluation.

Reports an interesting 'cross-modal regularization effect' finding (better textual supervision improves alignment across other modalities too), supported by a caption-source ablation (Table 3), offering a useful empirical insight for future dataset design.
weaknesses: The instruction-following benchmark (T2A-bench) and its automated judge both rely on the same Gemini 2.5 Pro model family that was also used to construct training annotations, creating potential circularity/self-consistency bias; no correlation study with independent human judgments is reported to validate the automated judge's reliability.

AudioX's SOTA claims in Table 1 conflate architectural contribution with a substantial training-data advantage (7M curated multimodal samples vs. baselines trained on smaller/standard datasets), making it hard to attribute gains specifically to the proposed MAF module versus sheer data scale; a controlled comparison (e.g., baselines fine-tuned on IF-caps) would strengthen the claims.

Quantitative improvements from the full MAF module over ablated variants (Table 4) are often marginal (e.g., IS 11.66 vs 11.84, FD 9.72 vs 9.64), and no statistical significance or variance is reported for these or the main benchmark comparisons.

Dataset quality relies entirely on automated LLM captioning (Gemini/Qwen2-Audio) without reported human verification of caption accuracy, which is a concern especially for complex, overlapping, or ambiguous audio scenes where hallucinated events/timestamps could introduce systematic label noise.

Details about a 'Private' dataset (175.2k clips) used for T2M training are not disclosed (source, licensing, content), raising reproducibility and provenance concerns; overlap between AudioTime train (20k) and test (2k) splits is not explicitly clarified, leaving potential leakage ambiguous.
The user study is relatively small in scale (25 samples per task, 10 raters) for the breadth of tasks claimed, limiting statistical robustness of the subjective SOTA claims.
Several figures (e.g., Fig. A.2, A.3, radar chart in Fig. 1) are visually cluttered with small, hard-to-read labels, reducing clarity of the presented comparisons.

Some directly relevant recent unified/any-to-any audio generation works mentioned in the introduction (e.g., Polyak et al. 2024, Zhang et al. 2024) are not included as quantitative baselines in the main comparison tables, leaving the positioning against the closest unified competitors somewhat incomplete.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely useful problem: unifying audio/music generation across flexible multimodal conditions (text, video, audio) rather than the common single-modality-in/single-domain-out setting.

A large, richly-annotated dataset (IF-caps, ~7M clips) is constructed via a structured Gemini+Qwen2-Audio annotation pipeline, and the authors commit to releasing it, which could be a useful community resource if released as promised.
The experimental scope is broad, covering T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, TV2M, audio inpainting, music completion, and image-to-audio, with both objective metrics and a human study.

The paper introduces a new instruction-following benchmark (T2A-bench) with fine-grained metrics (category, count, ordering, timestamp accuracy) that, if validated independently, addresses a real gap in existing T2A evaluation.
Ablations on caption source (Labels/AudioSetCaps/QwenCap/GeminiCap/GeminiCap-aug) and MAF components (gate/query) are provided, giving some insight into design choices.
weaknesses: Strong circularity/bias concern in evaluation: the training captions (IF-caps) are generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro, the new T2A-bench prompts are generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro, and the automated judge for T2A-bench is also Gemini 2.5 Pro. A model trained on Gemini-style captions being scored by a Gemini-based judge on Gemini-generated prompts is a self-referential evaluation loop that likely inflates AudioX's apparent instruction-following advantage over baselines that never saw this caption style or the judge's stylistic biases; no control experiment (e.g., a baseline retrained on the same IF-caps data, or a non-Gemini judge/human validation of the automated judge) is provided to rule this out.

The claimed 'SOTA across the majority of metrics' is only partially supported by Table 1 itself: e.g., on VGGSound V2A, AudioX has worse KL (2.21) than FRIEREN (1.40) and worse FAD (6.21) than several baselines (5.85, 5.89); on AVVP V2A, FAD (17.2) is far worse than most baselines. Many rows show AudioX winning on 1-2 metrics while losing on others, which is understated in the text's uniformly positive narrative.

The comparisons are not clearly controlled for data scale: AudioX is trained on a much larger, newly curated 7M-sample multimodal dataset, while baselines are evaluated using their original public checkpoints/training data. This confounds whether gains stem from the proposed architecture (MAF) versus simply more/better training data, undermining the paper's architectural contribution claims.

The 'cross-modal regularization effect' is a central claimed insight, but the empirical support (Table 3) shows quite small deltas (e.g., Cat-acc 28.05→28.91, Ord-acc 7.60→7.80) between GeminiCap and GeminiCap-aug, which is a modest and possibly noise-level difference to support a strong conceptual claim highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

The MAF module (per-modality gates + cross-attention queries + self-attention fusion) is architecturally incremental relative to well-established gated fusion and cross-attention mechanisms used in prior multimodal transformers; the paper does not clearly differentiate it from these prior designs beyond application context.

Reproducibility is limited at submission time: code and datasets are stated as 'will be available,' and key details (exact prompts to Gemini/Qwen2-Audio, benchmark judge prompts beyond illustrative examples, full hyperparameter search, random seeds, variance across runs) are not reported, making independent verification difficult.

The human study is fairly small in scope (10 experts, 25 samples per task) with no reported inter-rater agreement or statistical significance testing, weakening confidence in the subjective SOTA claims.

Several qualitative figures (e.g., spectrogram comparisons) are presented without objective quantitative backing for the specific claims made in the captions (e.g., 'uniquely excels' at ticking sounds), relying on visual impression rather than measurable evidence.

The paper's framing overstates novelty of 'unified anything-to-audio' generation, given that prior works (e.g., NExT-GPT, Polyak et al. 2024, Zhang et al. 2024) already explore multi-input unification; the differentiation from these baselines is mostly asserted rather than rigorously benchmarked against the most directly comparable unified baselines under matched training conditions.

strengths: Proposes a genuinely unified anything-to-audio framework (AudioX) that handles text, video, and audio conditioning for both general audio and music generation within a single DiT-based model, addressing a real gap where most prior work is single-modality or single-domain.

Constructs a large-scale (7M+ sample) multimodal dataset (JF-caps) via a structured two-stage annotation pipeline (Gemini 2.5 Pro for rich structured captions + Qwen2-Audio for cost-effective augmentation/diversification), which is a valuable resource if released.

Introduces a lightweight Multimodal Adaptive Fusion (MAF) module with gating and cross-attention query mechanisms, supported by a reasonably thorough architectural ablation (Table 4) showing each component contributes to performance.

Very broad experimental coverage: T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, TV2M, audio inpainting, music completion, and zero-shot image-to-audio, benchmarked against many strong, recent specialist baselines (MMAudio, Tango2, Stable Audio Open, FoleyCrafter, VidMuse, etc.), with mostly SOTA or highly competitive results.

Introduces a new instruction-following benchmark (T2A-bench) with a well-specified automated two-step LLM-judge evaluation pipeline, plus results on the existing AudioTime benchmark, providing fine-grained (category/count/order/timestamp) evaluation that is often missing in this literature.

Includes a professional (10-expert) subjective user study in addition to objective metrics, and an interesting ablation isolating the effect of caption/data quality ("cross-modal regularization effect"), offering a useful empirical insight for future dataset design.

Extensive appendix with dataset schema/examples, additional inpainting/completion/image-to-audio results, and qualitative spectrogram comparisons, aiding transparency and reproducibility of the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/bias in evaluation: Gemini 2.5 Pro is used both to construct the training data (JF-caps captions) and as the automated judge for the new T2A-bench and for generating benchmark prompts; this dual role is not discussed as a possible source of favorable bias toward a model trained on Gemini-style captions, and no cross-check with an independent judge/human agreement study for T2A-bench is reported.

The main comparison in Table 1 pits AudioX (trained on a much larger, curated 7M-sample dataset) against baselines trained on their original (often smaller) datasets; the gains could be substantially attributable to additional training data/compute rather than the architectural contribution (MAF), and this scale confound is not isolated (the caption-source ablation in Table 3 controls for caption quality but not for overall data volume/coverage).

No human verification or quality/error-rate analysis of the LLM-generated (Gemini/Qwen2-Audio) annotations is reported, so the actual noise level and reliability of the 7M-sample JF-caps dataset—central to the paper's claims—remains unquantified.

MAF ablation results are somewhat mixed (e.g., "w/o Gate" outperforms "Full MAF" on IS and FAD in Table 4), which is not discussed or explained, slightly undercutting the claimed necessity of each component.

Reliance on a costly proprietary model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for both data curation and benchmark construction/evaluation limits reproducibility and independent verification by the community, despite promises to release code/data.

No discussion of inference efficiency/compute cost relative to baselines (250 diffusion steps, 2.4B parameters, 4k H800 GPU-hours), which is relevant given the practical deployment motivation stated in the introduction.
The paper lacks a dedicated limitations/failure-case discussion; for instance, in the image-to-audio zero-shot experiment AudioX has weaker FD than some baselines and this trade-off is not analyzed.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting across the many benchmark tables, making it harder to assess whether reported improvements over close baselines (e.g., MMAudio) are meaningful.
